{{short description|Class of operator mapping}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''nonlocal [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]]''' is a [[Mapping (mathematics)|mapping]] that maps a space of functions on a topological space to another space of functions on some domain in such a way that the value of the function output at a given point cannot be determined solely from the values of the input function in an arbitrary neighbourhood of any point. An example of a nonlocal operator is the [[Fourier transform]].

== Formal definition ==

Let <math>X</math> be a [[topological space]], <math>Y</math> a [[Set (mathematics)|set]], <math>F(X)</math> a [[function space]] containing functions with [[Domain of a function|domain]] <math>X</math>, and <math>G(Y)</math> a function space containing functions with domain {{tmath|Y}}. Two functions <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> in <math>F(X)</math> are called equivalent at <math>x\in X</math> if there exists a [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] <math>N</math> of <math>x</math> such that <math>u(x')=v(x')</math> for all {{tmath|x'\in N}}. An operator <math>A: F(X) \to G(Y)</math> is said to be local if for every <math>y\in Y</math> there exists an <math>x\in X</math> such that <math>Au(y) = Av(y)</math> for all functions <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> in <math>F(X)</math> which are equivalent at {{tmath|x}}. A nonlocal operator is an operator which is not local.

For a local operator it is possible (in principle) to compute the value <math>Au(y)</math> using only knowledge of the values of <math>u</math> in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of a point {{tmath|x}}. For a nonlocal operator this is not possible.

== Examples ==

[[Differential operator]]s are examples of local operators. A large class of (linear) nonlocal operators is given by the [[integral transform]]s, such as the Fourier transform and the [[Laplace transform]]. For an integral transform of the form
: <math> (Au)(y) = \int \limits_X u(x)\, K(x, y)\, dx,</math>
where <math>K</math> is some kernel function, it is necessary to know the values of <math>u</math> almost everywhere on the [[Support (mathematics)|support]] of <math>K(\cdot, y)</math> in order to compute the value of <math>Au</math> at {{tmath|y}}.

An example of a [[singular integral operator]] is the [[fractional Laplacian]]
: <math> (-\Delta)^sf(x) = c_{d,s} \int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^d} \frac{f(x)-f(y)}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dy. </math>
The prefactor <math> c_{d,s} := \frac{4^s\Gamma(d/2+s)}{\pi^{d/2}|\Gamma(-s)|}</math> involves the [[Gamma function]] and serves as a normalizing factor. The fractional Laplacian plays a role in, for example, the study of nonlocal [[minimal surfaces]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Caffarelli |first1=L. |author-link=Luis Caffarelli |last2=Roquejoffre |first2=J.-M. |last3=Savin |first3=O. |date=2010 |title=Nonlocal minimal surfaces |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |volume=63 |issue=9 |pages=1111–1144 |language=en |doi=10.1002/cpa.20331|arxiv=0905.1183 |s2cid=10480423 }}</ref>

== Applications ==

Some examples of applications of nonlocal operators are:
* [[Time series]] analysis using Fourier transformations
* Analysis of [[dynamical systems]] using Laplace transformations
* [[Image denoising]] using [[non-local means]]<ref>{{Cite book |contribution=A Non-Local Algorithm for Image Denoising |last1=Buades |first1=A. |last2=Coll |first2=B. |last3=Morel |first3=J.-M. |date=2005 |title=2005 IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR'05) |publisher=IEEE |isbn=9780769523729 |volume=2 |location=San Diego, CA, USA |pages=60–65 |doi=10.1109/CVPR.2005.38|s2cid=11206708 }}</ref>
* Modelling [[Gaussian blur]] or [[motion blur]] in images using [[convolution]] with a [[Kernel (image processing)|blurring kernel]] or [[point spread function]]
